##converting dates to numbers:

coerce_date <- function(x) {
  x <- trimws(as.character(x))
  out <- suppressWarnings(ymd(x))
  if (all(is.na(out))) out <- suppressWarnings(dmy(x))
  if (all(is.na(out))) out <- suppressWarnings(mdy(x))
  if (all(is.na(out))) out <- suppressWarnings(readr::parse_date(x,
                      locale = locale(date_names = "en")))
  as.Date(out)
}
## cleaning data all across all column

df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    Traded        = coerce_date(Traded),
    Filed         = coerce_date(Filed),
    last_modified = coerce_date(last_modified)
  ) # write_csv(df, "project_clean.csv")

## Converting trade size usd into intervall

# Robust function to handle vectors properly
parse_min_max <- function(x) {
  # If x is NA or empty (works for vectors of length 1)
  if (length(x) != 1 || is.na(x) || trimws(x) == "") return(c(min = NA, max = NA))
  
  # Remove $ and commas
  x_clean <- gsub("[$,]", "", as.character(x))
  
  # Extract all numbers (integer or decimal)
  nums <- as.numeric(unlist(regmatches(x_clean, gregexpr("[0-9]+\\.?[0-9]*", x_clean))))
  
  # If no numbers found
  if (length(nums) == 0) return(c(min = NA, max = NA))
  
  # Return min and max
  c(min = min(nums, na.rm = TRUE), max = max(nums, na.rm = TRUE))
}

# Apply to the entire column safely
parsed <- t(sapply(as.character(df$Trade_Size_USD), parse_min_max))
parsed <- as.data.frame(parsed)

# Add min and max columns to your dataframe
df$Trade_Size_USD_min <- parsed$min
df$Trade_Size_USD_max <- parsed$max


##total number of trades :

length(df$Trade_Size_USD_min)


##average trade size :

mean(c(mean(df$Trade_Size_USD_min,na.rm = TRUE), mean(df$Trade_Size_USD_max,na.rm = TRUE)))

## Creating Net Trade Direction

df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    net_trade_direction = case_when(
      Transaction == "Purchase"           ~ 1,
      Transaction %in% c("Sale", "Sale (Partial)", "Sale (Full)") ~ -1,
      Transaction == "Exchange"           ~ 0,   # or NA_real_ if you prefer
      TRUE                                     ~ NA_real_
    )
  )

head(df[, c("Transaction", "net_trade_direction")])

total_direction <- sum(df$net_trade_direction, na.rm = TRUE)
total_direction

## Creating Midpoint for Trade Size

df <- df %>%
  mutate(
    trade_size_mid = (Trade_Size_USD_min + Trade_Size_USD_max)/2
  )

##Count trades by State × Chamber × Party

#Summarize counts
state_chamber_party <- df %>%
  group_by(State, Chamber, Party) %>%
  summarise(Num_Trades = n(), .groups = 'drop') %>%
  arrange(State, Chamber, desc(Num_Trades))

head(state_chamber_party)

#If we want to see party dominance as percentages within each state/chamber:

state_chamber_party <- state_chamber_party %>%
  group_by(State, Chamber) %>%
  mutate(Total_Trades = sum(Num_Trades),
         Party_Percent = Num_Trades / Total_Trades * 100)
         
##Visualize with a stacked bar chart       

ggplot(state_chamber_party, aes(x = State, y = Party_Percent, fill = Party)) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ Chamber) +  # separate House and Senate
  labs(y = "Percentage of Trades", title = "Party Distribution by State and Chamber") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
  
##Dominant Party

##Creating a Heatmap

library(ggplot2)

## Heatmap for dominant party in each state by house and senate

# Determine dominant party per State/Chamber (without the percentage, just the party that dominates)
dominant_party <- state_chamber_party %>%
  group_by(State, Chamber) %>%
  slice_max(order_by = Num_Trades, n = 1) %>%
  ungroup()
  
#Creating heatmap

ggplot(dominant_party, aes(x = State, y = Chamber, fill = Party)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("D" = "blue", "R" = "red")) +
  labs(title = "Dominant Party by State and Chamber",
       x = "State",
       y = "Chamber") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
  
##Heatmap (intensity)
library(ggplot2)
library(dplyr)

# Create a signed percent: Democrat = positive, Republican = negative
state_chamber_party <- state_chamber_party %>%
  mutate(Party_Signed_Percent = ifelse(Party == "D", Party_Percent, -Party_Percent))

#Creating Heatmap
ggplot(state_chamber_party, aes(x = State, y = Chamber, fill = Party_Signed_Percent)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  scale_fill_gradient2(
    low = "red",       # Republican
    mid = "white",     # neutral
    high = "blue",     # Democrat
    midpoint = 0,
    limits = c(-100, 100),
    name = "% of Trades\n(Red=R, Blue=D)"
  ) +
  labs(title = "Party Dominance Heatmap by State and Chamber",
       x = "State",
       y = "Chamber") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
  
##Excess return by Party

df %>%
  group_by(Party) %>%
  summarise(
    Mean_Excess_Return = mean(excess_return, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median_Excess_Return = median(excess_return, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD_Excess_Return = sd(excess_return, na.rm = TRUE),
    Num_Trades = n()
  )
  
## The results are very negative which is weird

summary(df$excess_return)

#A lot of NA's messing with the numbers, lets ignore them

mean(df$excess_return, na.rm = TRUE)    # mean ignoring NAs
median(df$excess_return, na.rm = TRUE)  # median ignoring NAs
sd(df$excess_return, na.rm = TRUE)      # standard deviation ignoring NAs

## Interpretation

# Mean = −15.03
# On average, trades underperformed the market benchmark by ~15%.
# This is slightly higher than the median because a few very large positive trades pull the mean up.

# Median = −27.71
# More than half of all trades underperformed the benchmark by ~28%.
# Confirms a negative skew: most trades lost relative to the market.

# SD = 179.91
# Extremely high variability → trade outcomes are very volatile.
# extreme outliers like 10,885 or −318 heavily influence dispersion.

##Histogram of Excess returns

library(ggplot2)

# Histogram limited to a reasonable range to visualize most trades
ggplot(df, aes(x = excess_return)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 100, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  xlim(-500, 500) +  # limits extreme outliers
  labs(title = "Distribution of Excess Return (Limited View)",
       x = "Excess Return",
       y = "Count") +
  theme_minimal()
  
##Who is overperforming?
#Which company?
#Which party?
#Which chamber?
#Which politician?

#Top overperformers (right tail) — highest excess return
df %>%
  filter(!is.na(excess_return)) %>%
  arrange(desc(excess_return)) %>%
  select(Name, Party, Company, Ticker, excess_return) %>%
  head(10)  # top 10 highest excess returns
